content.scenario: Yara runs a message relay service for activists in a country where digital messages can be used as evidence. Her system has three functions that create different message types: text, voice memo, and location pin. She cannot edit the three message-creation functions directly because they live in a shared library that five other apps depend on. Changing them would break those apps. She needs a way to wrap each function so that it still does its original job but also sets an expiration timer. content.scenario: Anika runs a small heritage homestay in Thanjavur and keeps a hand-written ledger of every pilgrim who stayed with her during the Brihadeeswara temple festival season. She needs to send a single printed sheet to the temple trust by Friday morning listing only the devotees who visited on the third day of the festival, and the ledger already has 230 entries.

stage1.prompt: Anika flips open her ledger. The pages are ruled into neat columns: name, village, day visited, donation amount. On day 3 alone there are forty-one rows. She runs her finger down the 'day visited' column, then across each row, copying names onto a separate sheet of paper.
stage1.guidingQuestion: What is Anika doing to the ledger, row by row, that takes her a long time by hand?

Reading the whole ledger once and remembering the day-3 names without writing them down.
attempt1.hint: If 230 entries arrived and she had to add day-4 names too, would her memory hold up? Try writing each one down instead of trusting your head.

attempt1.text: Recopying every single row, including the day-1 and day-2 pilgrims, onto the new sheet.
attempt1.hint: The trust asked for only day-3 visitors. What happens to the paper Anika hands over if it includes everyone?

stage3.conceptIdea: A short way to take a whole collection, keep only the items that match a rule, and reshape each kept item into a new list, all in one step.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python calls this shape a list comprehension: an expression applied to every item in a collection, with an optional condition, all written inside square brackets.
stage4.codeTemplate:
day_3_names = [pilgrim["name"] ___ pilgrim ___ ledger ___ pilgrim["day"] ___ 3]
print(day_3_names)

flowSteps.label: Python looks at ledger, the collection of all 230 pilgrim rows.
It pulls out one pilgrim at a time and assigns it to pilgrim.
It checks whether pilgrim["day"] is equal to 3. Rows that fail are skipped.
For each row that passes, it grabs pilgrim["name"] and collects it.

stage4.conceptReveal: In Python, that short name that stands in for a value is called a variable. You write it with the name on the left, an equals sign, then the value.

students = ___
print(students, "students signed up.")
print(students, "students will perform.")
print(students, "students need chairs.")

tokens.hint: If the value were the name itself, what number would get printed?
Quotes would make it a piece of text, not a number Miles could change with arithmetic later.

flowSteps.label: Line 1 runs first: Python sees the name students, then the equals sign, then 47.
flowSteps.note: Python stores 47 under the name students, like writing a label on a jar.

flowSteps.label: Line 2 runs: Python looks up students, finds 47, and prints 47 students signed up.
Line 3 runs: Python looks up students again, still finds 47, and prints 47 students will perform.
Line 4 runs: same lookup, same value, prints 47 students need chairs.
If Miles later writes students = 200 on line 1, every print below it would say 200 instead.
flowSteps.note: One change in one place updates every sentence that uses the name.

content.levelTitle: Kofi's Notebook: Two Ways to Repeat
content.designNote: The scenario needs two genuinely different reasons to repeat an action: a fixed known count and an unknown count driven by a target, so the boundary between the two ideas stays sharp instead of blurry. One level is enough here because the whole point is a single either/or decision, not a progression of difficulty.
content.scenario: Kofi Boateng runs a mobile phone-credit stand outside Kaneshie Market in Accra. Every morning before opening, he tops up credit for exactly 8 regular customers who prepaid the night before, working straight down his notebook list. During the day, when someone pays with a big note, he counts loose coins from his cash box into their hand one at a time until the change reaches the exact amount owed. He never knows ahead of time how many coins that will take, since it depends on what note they hand him and what they bought.

stage1.prompt: Here is a page from Kofi's notebook: a numbered list of his 8 morning customers, and beside it, a tally he scratched out while counting coins for Ama, one mark per coin, six marks total, stopping the moment the pile hit 13 cedis.
stage1.guidingQuestion: Look at how Kofi knows when to stop in each case. What's different?

attempt1.text: In the customer list he stops after the 8th name no matter what; with the coins he stops whenever the pile reaches 13 cedis, whether that takes 4 coins or 14.
Both are just Kofi repeating an action several times until he's done, so there's no real difference between them.
attempt1.hint: If Ama had paid with a note that needed 40 coins instead of 6, would counting them work the same way as going down a fixed list of 8 names?

attempt1.text: The customer list involves repeating an action, but counting coins is just one single action, not something that repeats.
attempt1.hint: If it takes six separate coins dropped one by one to reach 13 cedis, is that really only one action?

stage3.conceptIdea: There are two basic ways to repeat a set of steps: one where you know the exact number of rounds before you start, like going through a list, and one where you keep going only as long as some condition stays true, like counting coins until you hit an amount, where you only find out how many rounds it took after you stop.

stage4.conceptReveal: Python has two different tools for this: a for loop walks through a known sequence a fixed number of times, and a while loop keeps going only as long as a condition stays true.
stage4.codeTemplate:
customers = ["Ama", "Kwame", "Yaw", "Efua", "Kojo", "Abena", "Kwabena", "Adjoa"]
___ name in customers:
    top_up(name)

change_given = 0
coins_used = 0
___ change_given < 13:
    change_given += 2
    coins_used += 1

tokens.hint: What if Kofi doesn't know in advance how many coins it will take, only that he must keep going while the pile is still short?

flowSteps.label: Python builds the customers list with all 8 names.
The for loop runs top_up(name) once for each name in customers, in order.
The for loop stops automatically right after Adjoa, the 8th name.
change_given and coins_used both start at 0.
The while loop checks change_given < 13 before every round, adding 2 and incrementing coins_used each time it's still true.
Once change_given reaches 14, the condition change_given < 13 is false, so the while loop stops.

predictOutput.question: After this code finishes running, what are the final values of coins_used and change_given?

options.text: coins_used is 7 and change_given is 14
coins_used is 6 and change_given is 13
options.hint: Since change_given jumps by 2 each time, can it ever land exactly on 13?

options.text: coins_used is 8 and change_given is 16
options.hint: Try tracing change_given step by step from 0, checking the condition before each add.

edgeCase.question: What happens if the line change_given += 2 is accidentally left out of the while loop's body?

options.text: change_given stays 0 forever, so the loop never stops
Python notices nothing changed and exits the loop after one round
options.hint: If nothing inside the loop body ever changes change_given, will the condition change_given < 13 ever become false on its own?

stage5.practicePrompt: Efua needs a loop to text each of her 5 fixed suppliers and a separate loop to hand back coins until a refund reaches 7 cedis, using the right tool for each job.
stage5.practiceTemplate:
suppliers = ["Yaa", "Kwesi", "Nana", "Esi", "Fiifi"]
___ supplier in suppliers:
    send_text(supplier)

refund_given = 0
___ refund_given < 7:
    refund_given += 1

practiceTokens.hint: What if Efua doesn't know ahead of time how many coins it will take to reach the refund?

applyCheck.prompt: Which situation actually needs one of these two repeating tools, rather than something simpler?

options.text: A radio host keeps announcing raffle numbers one by one until someone finally shouts that they've won, with no idea in advance how many numbers that will take.
A shop clerk prints a single receipt for one sale.
options.hint: Is anything here actually repeating, or is it just one action happening once?

options.text: A courier already knows he has exactly 3 packages today and drives to each address once.
options.hint: With only 3 stops known in advance, could you just write out the 3 steps by hand instead of setting up a repeating tool?

content.scaleReflection: If Kofi's supplier list grew from 5 to 500, and refunds could still stop at any random coin, would you still trust a for loop for the list and a while loop for the refund, or would something about your reasoning need to change?
